API: Application Programming Interface: a defined set of requests and responses that lets one piece of software use another.
SDK: Software Development Kit: a bundle of libraries, tools, and docs for building software on a specific platform or service.
SSH: Secure Shell: an encrypted protocol for logging into and running commands on a remote machine.
HTTP: Hypertext Transfer Protocol: the request/response protocol web browsers and servers use to exchange data.
DNS: Domain Name System: the internet's directory that translates domain names like example.com into IP addresses.
TCP: Transmission Control Protocol: a network protocol that delivers data reliably and in order between two machines.
REST: Representational State Transfer: a style of web API design built around resources, URLs, and standard HTTP methods.
JSON: JavaScript Object Notation: a lightweight text format for structured data made of objects, arrays, strings, and numbers.
SQL: Structured Query Language: the standard language for querying and modifying relational databases.
CI/CD: Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery: automatically building, testing, and shipping code whenever changes are pushed.
CPU: Central Processing Unit: the general-purpose processor that executes a computer's instructions.
GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: a processor with thousands of parallel cores, widely used to train and run neural networks.
TPU: Tensor Processing Unit: Google's custom chip designed specifically to accelerate machine learning workloads.
CUDA: NVIDIA's platform and API for running general-purpose computations on its GPUs.
container: A lightweight, isolated package of an application and its dependencies that runs consistently across environments.
Kubernetes: An open-source system for deploying, scaling, and managing containerized applications across clusters of machines.
latency: The delay between a request being made and its response arriving, usually measured in milliseconds.
cache: A fast storage layer that keeps copies of frequently used data so future requests are served quicker.
hashing: Mapping data of any size to a fixed-size value, used for lookups, integrity checks, and password storage.
encryption: Encoding data so that only parties holding the right key can read it.
compiler: A program that translates source code into machine code or another lower-level form before it runs.
recursion: A technique where a function solves a problem by calling itself on smaller instances of the same problem.
AI: Artificial Intelligence: the field of building systems that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence.
ML: Machine Learning: building systems that learn patterns from data instead of following explicitly programmed rules.
machine learning: Building systems that learn patterns from data instead of following explicitly programmed rules.
deep learning: Machine learning using neural networks with many layers to learn increasingly abstract features from data.
neural network: A model made of layers of interconnected nodes whose weighted connections are tuned from data.
LLM: Large Language Model: a neural network trained on vast amounts of text to understand and generate language.
NLP: Natural Language Processing: the field of getting computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language.
transformer: A neural network architecture built on attention, the basis of most modern language models.
attention: A mechanism that lets a model weigh how relevant each part of the input is when processing another part.
embedding: A list of numbers (a vector) representing an item such as a word or document so that similar items sit close together.
vector database: A database optimized for storing embeddings and quickly finding the vectors most similar to a query.
token: A chunk of text, often a word or word piece, that a language model reads and generates one at a time.
tokenizer: The component that splits raw text into tokens and maps them to numeric IDs for a model.
context window: The maximum number of tokens a language model can take into account at once.
prompt: The input text or instructions given to a generative AI model to steer its output.
RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: fetching relevant documents at query time and giving them to an LLM so its answer is grounded in them.
inference: Running a trained model on new inputs to produce predictions or outputs, as opposed to training it.
training: The process of adjusting a model's parameters on data so its predictions improve.
fine-tuning: Further training a pretrained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset to specialize it.
LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation: a fine-tuning method that trains small add-on matrices instead of all of a model's weights.
quantization: Storing a model's weights with fewer bits (e.g. 8 or 4 instead of 16) to shrink it and speed up inference.
distillation: Training a smaller "student" model to imitate a larger "teacher" model's outputs.
hallucination: When a generative model produces confident-sounding output that is false or not supported by its input.
overfitting: When a model memorizes its training data so closely that it performs poorly on new, unseen data.
gradient descent: An optimization method that repeatedly nudges parameters in the direction that most reduces the error.
backpropagation: The algorithm that computes how much each weight in a neural network contributed to the error, so it can be updated.
loss function: A formula that scores how wrong a model's predictions are; training tries to minimize it.
epoch: One complete pass through the entire training dataset.
hyperparameter: A setting chosen before training, like learning rate or batch size, rather than learned from data.
benchmark: A standardized test or dataset used to measure and compare the performance of systems or models.
CNN: Convolutional Neural Network: a network that uses sliding filters to detect patterns, commonly used for images.
RNN: Recurrent Neural Network: a network that processes sequences step by step while carrying a hidden state forward.
GAN: Generative Adversarial Network: two networks, a generator and a discriminator, trained against each other to produce realistic data.
diffusion model: A generative model that creates data, such as images, by learning to gradually remove noise from random input.
reinforcement learning: Training an agent by rewarding or penalizing its actions as it interacts with an environment.
RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: tuning a model using human preference ratings as the reward signal.
agent: An AI system that plans and takes actions, such as calling tools or APIs, to accomplish a goal.
Git: A distributed version control system that tracks changes to files and lets many people work on the same code.
Docker: A tool for building and running applications inside containers.
microservices: An architecture that splits an application into small, independently deployable services that talk over a network.
load balancer: A system that spreads incoming traffic across multiple servers so no single one is overwhelmed.
CDN: Content Delivery Network: servers spread around the world that deliver web content from a location close to the user.
TLS: Transport Layer Security: the encryption protocol that secures connections such as HTTPS.
HTTPS: HTTP sent over an encrypted TLS connection, protecting data from eavesdropping and tampering.
OAuth: An authorization standard that lets an app access your data on another service without seeing your password.
JWT: JSON Web Token: a compact, signed token used to prove identity or permissions between systems.
CORS: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: browser rules that control which websites may request data from a different domain.
WebSocket: A protocol that keeps a two-way connection open between browser and server for real-time data.
GraphQL: A query language for APIs where the client asks for exactly the fields it needs in a single request.
gRPC: A high-performance framework for calling functions on remote services, using Protocol Buffers for messages.
CLI: Command-Line Interface: a text-based way to interact with a program by typing commands.
IDE: Integrated Development Environment: an application that combines a code editor, debugger, and build tools.
regex: Regular expression: a compact pattern language for searching and matching text.
Big O notation: A way to describe how an algorithm's time or memory use grows as its input gets larger.
hash table: A data structure that maps keys to values using a hash function, giving near-constant-time lookups.
binary search: Finding an item in a sorted list by repeatedly halving the range that could contain it.
linked list: A data structure where each element points to the next, making insertions cheap but random access slow.
garbage collection: Automatic memory management that frees memory a program is no longer using.
race condition: A bug where a program's result depends on the unpredictable timing of concurrent operations.
deadlock: A situation where two or more processes wait on each other forever, so none can proceed.
mutex: Mutual exclusion lock: ensures only one thread at a time can access a shared resource.
idempotent: Describes an operation that has the same effect whether it runs once or many times.
serverless: A cloud model where the provider runs your code on demand and you don't manage servers.
virtual machine: Software that emulates a complete computer, letting one physical machine run several isolated operating systems.
VPN: Virtual Private Network: an encrypted tunnel that routes your internet traffic through another server.
IP address: A numeric label identifying a device on a network so data can be routed to it.
open source: Software whose source code is publicly available for anyone to use, study, modify, and share.
technical debt: The future cost of rework caused by choosing a quick or easy solution now.
refactoring: Restructuring existing code to improve its design without changing what it does.
unit test: An automated test that checks a small, isolated piece of code, such as a single function.
NoSQL: Databases that store data in formats other than relational tables, such as documents or key-value pairs.
ORM: Object-Relational Mapping: a library that lets code work with database rows as regular objects.
SaaS: Software as a Service: software delivered over the internet on a subscription instead of installed locally.
WebAssembly: A compact binary format that lets code written in languages like C++ or Rust run in the browser at near-native speed.
DOM: Document Object Model: the browser's tree representation of a web page that scripts can read and change.
supervised learning: Training a model on labeled examples so it learns to predict the label for new inputs.
unsupervised learning: Finding patterns or structure in data without labeled answers.
clustering: Grouping data points so that items in the same group are more similar to each other than to others.
feature engineering: Creating or transforming input variables to help a model learn more effectively.
dropout: A training technique that randomly disables neurons to prevent a network from overfitting.
learning rate: A hyperparameter controlling how big each update step is during training.
batch size: The number of training examples processed together before the model's weights are updated.
activation function: A function applied to a neuron's output, such as ReLU, that lets networks learn non-linear patterns.
ReLU: Rectified Linear Unit: an activation function that outputs the input if positive and zero otherwise.
softmax: A function that turns a list of scores into probabilities that add up to 1.
logits: The raw, unnormalized scores a model outputs before they are converted into probabilities.
BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers: a Google language model that reads text in both directions.
GPT: Generative Pre-trained Transformer: a family of language models that generate text by predicting the next token.
mixture of experts: A model design where a router sends each input to a few specialized sub-networks instead of the whole model.
MoE: Mixture of Experts: a model design where a router sends each input to a few specialized sub-networks.
zero-shot: Performing a task without being shown any examples of it.
few-shot: Performing a task after being shown only a handful of examples, often inside the prompt.
chain-of-thought: Prompting or training a model to reason through intermediate steps before giving a final answer.
prompt engineering: Designing and refining the instructions given to an AI model to get better results.
perplexity: A measure of how well a language model predicts text; lower means less 'surprised'.
cosine similarity: A measure of how similar two vectors are based on the angle between them.
semantic search: Search that matches by meaning, typically using embeddings, rather than exact keywords.
multimodal: Describes models that work with more than one kind of data, such as text, images, and audio.
foundation model: A large model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks.
AGI: Artificial General Intelligence: hypothetical AI able to match humans across nearly all intellectual tasks.
guardrails: Rules and checks placed around an AI system to keep its behavior safe and on-task.
synthetic data: Artificially generated data used to train or test models in place of, or alongside, real data.
data augmentation: Creating modified copies of training data, like rotated images, to make a model more robust.
F1 score: A single accuracy metric that balances precision (how many predictions were right) and recall (how many true cases were found).
confusion matrix: A table comparing a classifier's predictions against actual labels, showing each kind of error.
cross-validation: Evaluating a model by repeatedly training on part of the data and testing on the rest.
PCA: Principal Component Analysis: reducing data to fewer dimensions while keeping as much variation as possible.
k-means: A clustering algorithm that splits data into k groups around repeatedly updated center points.
decision tree: A model that makes predictions by following a series of yes/no questions about the input.
random forest: An ensemble of many decision trees whose predictions are combined for better accuracy.
XGBoost: A popular, fast gradient-boosted decision tree library, widely used for tabular data.
MLOps: Practices and tooling for deploying, monitoring, and maintaining machine learning models in production.
model drift: The decline in a model's accuracy over time as real-world data changes from what it was trained on.
encoder: The part of a model that converts input into an internal numeric representation.
decoder: The part of a model that turns an internal representation into output, such as generated text.
self-attention: Attention where every token in a sequence looks at every other token in the same sequence.
positional encoding: Information added to token embeddings so a transformer knows the order of words.
KV cache: Stored attention keys and values from earlier tokens, reused so a model doesn't recompute them at each generation step.
speculative decoding: Speeding up generation by having a small model draft tokens that a larger model verifies in bulk.
MCP: Model Context Protocol: an open standard for connecting AI assistants to external tools and data sources.
vision transformer: A transformer that processes images by splitting them into patches treated like tokens.
